title: MotionShift: Environment-Compatible Motion Transfer via Planner-Evaluator Synergistic Adaptation
shortTitle: MotionShift: Environment-Compatible Motion Transfer via Planner-Evaluator Synergistic Adaptation
abstract: Existing motion transfer methods excel at exact, rigid motion replication from reference videos to target scenes, whereas they often fail to account for the compatibility between the transferred motion and the target scene environment in accordance with physical laws. In this work, we propose MotionShift, a novel motion transfer framework that achieves high-fidelity motion transfer while ensuring physical compatibility with the target scene. In particular, we design a planner--evaluator iterative motion adaptation mechanism, in which a Large Language Model (LLM) acts as the planner to generate motion trajectories by leveraging its strong semantic reasoning capabilities, while a Vision-Language Model (VLM) serves as the evaluator to rectify the motion based on its superior visual perception and scene understanding. Through this planner--evaluator synergistic reasoning process, the motion is adapted to the target scene in a training-free manner. The adapted motion is then used as a generative condition for an image-to-video (I2V) model to render videos in the target scene. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MotionShift achieves high-fidelity and physically compatible motion transfer across diverse and complex scenes. Moreover, we show that MotionShift can be readily integrated into existing trajectory-conditioned I2V models, endowing them with realistic motion transfer capabilities.

title: World Model Interpretability: From Decoding Representations to Understanding Latent Worlds
shortTitle: World Model Interpretability: From Decoding Representations to Understanding Latent Worlds
abstract: Emerging Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) are moving beyond representation learning towards latent world models that support prediction, planning, and control. Yet their latent worlds naturally lack a human-interpretable interface. In this Perspective, we argue that as JEPA latents become internal states for prediction and action, interpretability must move beyond what they encode to how latent variables interact, evolve, and causally drive prediction. To this end, we envision a four-stage research agenda, involving Ground, Structure, Verify, and Act, to guide this shift toward actionable latent-world understanding. Within our framework, existing JEPA interpretability efforts provide early evidence for Ground, while systematic analysis of latent structure, causal verification, and intervention remains largely unexplored. Overall, this Perspective aims to call for a broader latent-world interpretability agenda that shifts attention from decoding representations toward understanding, validating, and acting on latent worlds.

title: Aligning Language Models with Indigenous Community Cosmovision through Constitutional AI
shortTitle: Aligning Language Models with Indigenous Community Cosmovision through Constitutional AI
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are predominantly trained on corpora that reflect Western, anglophone worldviews. This asymmetry is not neutral: when a model answers questions about territory, community authority, or the relationship with nature, it does so from assumptions that may be alien to the communities using the system. This paper presents a system for aligning language models with the ethical principles of Indigenous communities in Latin America. Drawing on interviews with five Indigenous leaders and defenders, we built an operational cultural constitution grounded in an Indigenous cosmovision, with 12 principles. On this basis, we implemented a Constitutional AI (CAI) pipeline in two phases: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and direct preference optimization (DPO). The base models were Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct. With only 24 preference pairs, improvements were modest but detectable in intergenerational transmission, linguistic caution, and consultation and consent. Qualitative analysis reveals that the SFT phase was responsible for the primary shift in alignment, while DPO refined specific categories. The system was deployed in a conversational interface with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) that allows communities to feed the knowledge base, turning alignment into a participatory cycle. We argue the architecture is functional and will scale qualitatively once the corpus is expanded and computing constraints are resolved. The work constitutes a first iteration of an epistemic justice mechanism for value alignment in the Global South.

title: Learning When to Abort in Transformer Planning: A Mechanistic Study
shortTitle: Learning When to Abort in Transformer Planning: A Mechanistic Study
abstract: Planning does not by itself imply the ability to recognise errors, but recognising errors can improve planning capacity. In this paper, we study this phenomenon in Transformer planning. To analyze the inner mechanism, we follow the approach of Wang et al. (2024) and abstract planning as path-finding in graphs. In this setting, we train the model to detect the error of invalid transitions, i.e., after the model generates a next node that is not adjacent with the current node, the model should then generate a special abort token x. For expressiveness, we construct a Transformer with feed-forward width $O(|V|)$ for any fixed graph with node set $V$. It can detect all possible invalid transitions, and select a valid next node if the prefix is valid. We then propose a worst-case lower bound on feed-forward width, which makes the detector's linear width near-optimal up to logarithmic factors. In trained models, we demonstrate that invalid-transition detection increases previous-node attention, and most of the valid--invalid separation locates in the feed-forward network's output. This accords with our theoretical insights. Finally, we use this error detection to improve the model's performance: at inference, generating the abort token x will directly cause an external procedure to discard the attempt and restart from the original prompt. Experiments show that error detection combined with retry improves model's planning reliability on graphs, Countdown, and mazes.

title: Shared-Private Cross-Modal Discrepancy Learning for Imbalanced Multi-Source Audio-Visual Deepfake Detection
shortTitle: Shared-Private Cross-Modal Discrepancy Learning for Imbalanced Multi-Source Audio-Visual Deepfake Detection
abstract: Audio-visual deepfake detectors are often trained under a single dataset or manipulation regime, but multi-source training collections may contain heterogeneous attacks and uneven source distributions. Training separate detectors for each source is inefficient, while a single shared detector may be biased toward dominant source-specific patterns. We study known-source imbalanced multi-source audio-visual deepfake detection using FakeAVCeleb and LAV-DF, where source identity is supplied during training and inference. To address this setting, we build on the Multi-Scale Cross-Modal Transformer Encoder (MSCT) and propose Pre-MSCT Shared-Private Feature Fusion. Our method routes \texttt{[CLS]}-augmented audio and visual tokens into a shared stream and source-specific private streams before the first MSCT block, while retaining its internal multi-scale self-attention (MSSA), differential cross-modal attention (DCA), and feed-forward operations. The shared stream models cross-source reusable evidence, while the private streams retain source-dependent residual variations. A domain-aware gated residual fusion module injects selected private evidence into the shared representation for the main fused prediction. Experiments under two controlled source-composition protocols show improved macro and worst-source AUC compared with the MRDF and MSCT baselines. These results support shared-private cross-modal discrepancy learning in the evaluated two-source setting with known source identity.

title: SENRI: Understanding the Space-Event Nexus in Real-Life Videos
shortTitle: SENRI: Understanding the Space-Event Nexus in Real-Life Videos
abstract: Human memories are organized in a way that connects events with their corresponding spatial contexts. An AI assistant should also be able to memorize and recall the nexus of events and spaces. Thus we introduce SENRI, a task that studies this space--event connection in long, continuous real-life egocentric video. It contains six task types in two directions: Event$\rightarrow$Space, which recovers spatial knowledge from event cues, and Space$\rightarrow$Event, which retrieves events from regions and trajectories. To evaluate this, we build SENRI-Bench, containing 500 manually annotated multiple-choice questions over 10 uninterrupted self-recorded videos with around 25.3 hours of content. Also, we evaluate three typical long video understanding paradigms: direct perception, evidence seeking, and persistent memory. The task remains challenging across all three paradigms, highlighting substantial room for improvement. Then we show two representative failure modes of existing memory methods and address these evidence gaps with SENRI-Agent, a controller that uses Target-Guided Visual Check (TGVC) to propose local visual check tasks for parallel verifiers and integrate the reports into a working memory to help with reasoning. Built upon existing memory systems, SENRI-Agent improves the performance of existing baselines without modifying their stored memories. We hope SENRI will provide valuable insights into how real-life egocentric understanding should be evaluated, reveal the gaps in existing approaches, and offer a possible direction for improvement.

title: Atoms, Not Knowledge: What Production-Scale Addressed-Memory Writes Deposit
shortTitle: Atoms, Not Knowledge: What Production-Scale Addressed-Memory Writes Deposit
abstract: Deterministic hash-addressed conditional memory permits local post-hoc knowledge injection. Extending arXiv:2610.21553's bounded-feasibility audit rejecting under-specified generality claims with repaired probes and training-dose/capacity axes, we give, to our knowledge, the first production-scale write-content verdict. We test 124M-7B self-trained/publicly pretrained beds, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP8 (176.95B; 320,001,536 FP8 rows), and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Write coverage requires a sufficiently trained backbone prior, full-width readout, trainable gates; undertrained-bed intervention confirms a threshold, not a slope. At fixed budget, coverage falls from 98% (50 facts) to 12.7% (1,000); table size is not binding. Two-hop composition does not exceed the independent single-hop baseline (26% observed vs 25% expected; 15% lexical-distortion floor). Synergy remains absent across dose/load in two independent bed families. A 28-percentage-point in-context gap (given vs recalled intermediates) localizes failure to retrieval-for-reasoning, not gate access. Writes are independently retrievable, precisely addressable, reversible atoms, not composable into reasoning. A layered protocol, the first, to our knowledge, to cover compositionality in behavioral memory evaluation, separates baseline, synergy and distortion floor. Any addressed/key-value memory must report coverage, synergy ratio and distortion rate before deployment claims. Composition must be system-orchestrated; multi-constraint queries should explicitly chain written atoms. In-context controls show given intermediate entities are exploited at twice the implicit rate. Production load fits exponential interference ($R^2=0.98$); its mechanism, between budget dilution and write interference, remains open. All numbers are recomputed from archived raw logs/JSON; a fresh 52-target production rerun gives 52/52, exactly matching archived baselines.

title: AdaFedXplain: Adaptive Federated Learning with Explainable AI for Ransomware Detection
shortTitle: AdaFedXplain: Adaptive Federated Learning with Explainable AI for Ransomware Detection
abstract: Attacks using ransomware have developed into complex multiphase campaigns that target vital infrastructure, resulting in annual damages of billions of dollars. Conventional detection techniques are ineffective against zero-day variations, and privacy issues are raised by centralized machine learning algorithms. Federated learning allows for cooperative model training without data sharing, however current FL approaches suffer from explainability issues, high communication cost, and non-IID data heterogeneity. In this study, we present AdaFedXplain, an explainable AI-based adaptive federated learning system for ransomware detection. Our approach includes progressive XGBoost complexity to avoid overfitting, a decaying learning rate schedule for stable convergence, and dynamic client grading based on ransomware prevalence and data sufficiency. Using 62,485 real-world ransomware samples from four OS-based non-IID clients, we compare AdaFedXplain against FedAvg, FedProx, and SCAFFOLD. According to experimental data, AdaFedXplain outperforms all baselines with 99.59% detection accuracy and 99.64% F1-score while cutting energy usage by 75%, latency by 65%, and communication overhead by 75%. The ablation investigation demonstrates that every element enhances performance. Security analysts can use SHAP explainability to identify important PE header characteristics that influence detection decisions. Our system provides a collaborative ransomware detection solution that is efficient and interpretable, while reducing privacy risks through federated learnings data-local training paradigm.

title: Where and Why Search-Augmented LLMs Fail When Reasoning over Rapidly Evolving Knowledge
shortTitle: Where and Why Search-Augmented LLMs Fail When Reasoning over Rapidly Evolving Knowledge
abstract: As the world changes, new information is published while older records remain online. This complicates reasoning for large language models (LLMs), which must retrieve evidence and resolve conflicts to determine which information remains valid. Existing evaluations treat information seeking as a black box, revealing little about where and why LLMs fail. To address this gap, we introduce TREK, a suite of three components: TREKTRACE is a plug-and-play framework that attributes failures to specific stages of retrieval and reasoning. We apply it to TREKBENCH-WILD, a meta-benchmark of real-world questions that require complex reasoning over rapidly evolving knowledge. Surprisingly, the main bottleneck is post-retrieval reasoning rather than retrieval: frontier models are often misled by conflicting evidence even after retrieving all the information needed to answer. To study this bottleneck, we build TREKBENCH-CTRL, a controlled benchmark with distractors spanning temporality, relevance, and trustworthiness, and show that benchmarks dominated by outdated distractors substantially underestimate task difficulty. Together, TREK provides a testbed for diagnosing and improving reasoning over rapidly evolving knowledge.

title: Where Groups Split: A Probe Prior for Nonzero Within-Group Variance in RL Post-Training
shortTitle: Where Groups Split: A Probe Prior for Nonzero Within-Group Variance in RL Post-Training
abstract: Group relative policy optimization learns from a prompt only when the rewards in the sampled group disagree. With a binary verifier, a group that is entirely correct or entirely incorrect has within-group variance zero and a zero advantage. Uniform sampling continues to spend rollouts on prompts that are unanimous now and stay unanimous as training goes on. Pass rate is a weak forecast of that future. Two prompts at the same pass rate can move apart: one into the range where a finite group splits, and one toward a ceiling where the group becomes unanimous again. Aperture estimates the later pass rate from a short probe. A small subset of the pool is trained with the same recipe, every prompt is scored on the base model and on the probe model, and the two pass rates are plugged into the probability that a group of the training size is all wrong or split. The resulting weight is a static prior. It can be used alone or multiplied by an online scheduler, and the GRPO update is left as it is. On mathematical and logical reasoning with 1.7B and 4B models, the prior improves greedy accuracy over uniform GRPO and raises the fraction of groups with a nonzero advantage. The same prior still helps when it is combined with dynamic sampling or with selective rollouts.

title: MPIG: Multi-angle Polarization Image Generation from a Single Polarization Observation
shortTitle: MPIG: Multi-angle Polarization Image Generation from a Single Polarization Observation
abstract: Polarization imaging provides informative cues for material analysis, scene understanding, and visual perception. However, acquiring complete polarization observations typically requires specialized hardware and multi-angle measurements, thereby increasing system complexity and limiting practical deployment. In this work, we address the problem of predicting the missing $45^\circ$, $90^\circ$, and $135^\circ$ polarization views from a single $0^\circ$ observation by leveraging a learned scene prior. To this end, we propose MPIG (Multi-angle Polarization Image Generation), a Swin Transformer-based framework that couples cross-angle feature interaction with residual decoding to predict angle-dependent intensity variations while preserving shared scene structure. Specifically, measured Stokes differences and polarization-strength-aware supervision guide the recovery of polarization modulation, orientation, and magnitude, while low-rank factorization further reduces the decoding cost. We also construct HighPol, a large-scale real-world polarization dataset comprising 5,474 groups of high-resolution four-angle polarization images collected from diverse indoor and outdoor scenes. Experimental results demonstrate improved image and polarization accuracy, achieving 29.729 dB PSNR, 0.9505 SSIM, and $21.514^\circ$ AoLP MAngE while requiring 85.86 M parameters and 1.126 T FLOPs. Furthermore, downstream validation on glass and semantic-segmentation tasks suggests that the generated polarization images can preserve task-relevant information, demonstrating the effectiveness of MPIG and the practical utility of predicted polarization observations for downstream vision applications.

title: CoRe-WM: Conditioned Response-State World Modeling for Longitudinal Treatment-Response Prediction in Breast DCE-MRI
shortTitle: CoRe-WM: Conditioned Response-State World Modeling for Longitudinal Treatment-Response Prediction in Breast DCE-MRI
abstract: Pathologic complete response (pCR) after neoadjuvant chemotherapy is a key prognostic indicator in aggressive breast cancer, yet existing prediction approaches either rely on pretreatment imaging alone, missing the patient's evolving response, or optimize multi-visit classifiers under direct outcome supervision, coupling representation learning with the clinical endpoint. We formulate longitudinal pCR prediction as a world-modeling problem and propose Conditioned Response-state World Modeling (CoRe-WM), which learns a latent state-transition model that predicts the next imaging state from the observed sequence. The transition function is conditioned on patient clinical profile and assigned therapy through additive shift and feature-wise modulation, enabling patient- and treatment-specific dynamics. A Factorized Response State pathway further decouples treatment-response dynamics from imaging appearance by encoding the structural prior that response manifests primarily in lesion morphology. After pretraining, all parameters are frozen and a linear readout predicts pCR at each clinical decision point. We evaluate CoRe-WM on I-SPY2 under five-fold cross-validation and assess cross-cohort transfer on I-SPY1. CoRe-WM achieves the highest discrimination among all evaluated methods at every prospective decision point, and demonstrates robust cross-cohort transfer. Ablation studies identify patient-profile conditioning and the factorized response pathway as the principal contributors. These results establish world-model-based representation learning as a promising framework for outcome prediction in oncology and beyond.

title: A Distribution-Free Separation Between Learned and Fixed Features
shortTitle: A Distribution-Free Separation Between Learned and Fixed Features
abstract: The success of neural networks is largely attributed to their ability to learn useful representations from training data. However, known results that prove a computational advantage of learned features over fixed ones are restricted to specific input distributions. We settle the COLT open question of Feldman, Kamath, and Srebro (2026) by showing that this advantage can persist in the distribution-free setting. We construct a family of hypothesis classes that can be efficiently learned by a natural gradient-based algorithm on a two-layer ReLU network, but cannot be represented by linear predictors over any fixed feature map with polynomial dimension (and runtime). Specifically, for any sufficiently small error and any sufficiently large runtime budget R (depending on the error), there exists a hypothesis class that the neural network learns under any input distribution to the desired expected classification error in time at most R, while the dimension complexity (governing the dimension needed by linear predictors) is superpolynomial in R.

title: Edge Deployable Lightweight Framework for Real-Time Driver Safety System with Integrated Lane Departure and Traffic Sign Recognition
shortTitle: Edge Deployable Lightweight Framework for Real-Time Driver Safety System with Integrated Lane Departure and Traffic Sign Recognition
abstract: Lane departure and traffic-sign negligence are leading contributors to road accidents, particularly in regions with non-standardized signage and limited annotated data. Existing Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) solutions are often developed as disjointed submodules, are rarely validated for real-time operation, and struggle to balance accuracy with low-latency inference for embedded deployment. We address these gaps with a unified, edge-deployable ADAS framework that simultaneously performs lane-departure warning (LDW) and traffic-sign detection and recognition (TSD/TSR), and validate the proposed system on automotive-class devices. Our framework combines a lightweight, lane-segmentation-driven LDW, which includes a drivable-area fallback for degraded markings, with a two-stage TSD/TSR pipeline consisting of efficient sign localization followed by fine-grained classification, designed to preserve accuracy at embedded latency. To support region-specific deployment under data scarcity, we curate a 35-class local traffic-sign dataset and introduce a generalized augmentation and balancing profile, expanding the corpus from 359 images to 8,750 samples. On an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano, the integrated system sustains 15 FPS end to end (32 FPS for LDW and 18 FPS for TSD/TSR). The TSD/TSR branch achieves 97.4 mAP for detection and 95.6% validation accuracy (93.1% on a local real-world set) while maintaining an approximately 13.9 M parameter footprint. Relative to recent methods that target a single task or report results only on desktop-class GPUs, our approach delivers both LDW and TSD/TSR with real-time performance on edge hardware, providing a practical pathway to low-cost, field-ready ADAS in resource-constrained settings.

title: Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention
shortTitle: Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention
abstract: Multi-head attention is a central component of the transformer architecture, yet how its expressivity depends on the number of heads remains poorly understood. We study a one-layer, attention-only transformer with additive positional embeddings and define the head complexity $H^\ast(f)$ of a Boolean function $f$ as the minimum number of attention heads required to represent it. We derive an exact linear-fractional normal form for head complexity, prove a general threshold-degree lower bound, and give an explicit ten-bit function for which this bound is strict. For symmetric Boolean functions, we independently show that head complexity equals the number of times the function changes value between consecutive Hamming-weight levels, even when positional embeddings are allowed. This agrees with the concurrent characterization of Hsu and Xu (arXiv:2608.04243) in a model without positional embeddings. The symmetric lower bound combines our general threshold-degree bound with the classical result of Aspnes et al. (1994). These results were discovered and formalized by a frontier model through conjecture generation, theorem proving, and machine verification, while human researchers asked the high-level questions and reviewed the generated theorems. We make the Lean formalization and research traces publicly available to support agent-assisted theorem proving and formal verification in mechanistic interpretability. This work provides a proof of concept for using the capabilities of frontier models, grounded by formal verification, to develop an understanding of transformer architectures.

title: CASE: Complementary Articulation-Aware Speech Encoder to Enhance Speech-Driven 3D Facial Animation
shortTitle: CASE: Complementary Articulation-Aware Speech Encoder to Enhance Speech-Driven 3D Facial Animation
abstract: General-purpose self-supervised speech encoders provide strong acoustic representations, but their pretraining objectives are not explicitly aligned with the visible articulatory dynamics required by speech-driven 3D facial animation. We propose CASE (Complementary Articulation-aware Speech Encoder), a complementary speech encoder adapted by contrastively aligning short speech clips with continuous 3D lip-mesh VQ-VAE latents. After adaptation, the geometry branch is removed, and the audio-only CASE representation is fused with the baseline SSL speech representation through residual cross-attention, while retaining the motion-decoder architecture and objective. Across four VOCASET baselines, CASE reduces mean lip vertex error by 2.8-6.0%, and mean full-face vertex error decreases in every system. Under the same fusion protocol, CASE yields lower mean LVE than the unadapted AV-SE stream on all four generators, with model-dependent margins. Because adaptation uses Korean speech-geometry pairs and evaluation uses English VOCASET, the result is consistent with cross-language downstream transfer under a shared English-pretrained audio-visual prior.

title: MCSplat: Multi-View Photometric and Geometric Consistent Feed-Forward Gaussian Splatting for Driving Scenes
shortTitle: MCSplat: Multi-View Photometric and Geometric Consistent Feed-Forward Gaussian Splatting for Driving Scenes
abstract: Driving-scene reconstruction via feed-forward Gaussian splatting from sparse multi-view images remains challenging due to two factors. First, cross-camera photometric inconsistency, caused by variations in exposure, ISP, and illumination, can be incorrectly absorbed into Gaussian geometry. Second, unreliable local geometric supervision arises from normal-based constraints near depth discontinuities. To address these issues, we present \textbf{MCSplat}, a multi-view consistent feed-forward Gaussian splatting framework for driving scenes. MCSplat constructs a canonical appearance space from depth-guided multi-camera correspondences to decouple geometry learning from camera-specific appearance. A multi-scale Bilateral Grid Transformer restores raw camera appearance from canonical renderings, enabling photometric supervision without contaminating Gaussian geometry. To improve local geometric reliability, we estimate Fisher-information-based uncertainty from photometric sensitivity and use it to adaptively weight surface-oriented self-supervision. Extensive experiments demonstrate improved reconstruction quality and generalization across driving datasets. Geometry-oriented evaluations further reveal enhanced cross-view depth consistency and local surface-normal agreement, while qualitative results show fewer geometric artifacts and more coherent structures across overlapping views.

title: Predicted Class Correction: Conformal Thresholds for Classes with No Calibration Data
shortTitle: Predicted Class Correction: Conformal Thresholds for Classes with No Calibration Data
abstract: Class-conditional conformal prediction calibrates a separate score threshold for every class and therefore requires labelled calibration examples of every class. In long-tailed deployments these are exactly what is missing: rare classes are left with few or no held-out examples, and existing methods are either undefined for them or fall back to the shared marginal threshold. We ask whether the per-class correction can instead be predicted from descriptors of the class that require no labels at all. We propose Predicted Class Correction (PCC), which regresses the offset between the per-class and the marginal conformal quantile on geometric descriptors of the classifier head, shrinks the prediction by a scalar selected on the labelled classes, and refits a single marginal offset. The descriptors depend only on the model's weights, so a class with zero calibration examples still receives its own threshold, and since only one scalar is calibrated, split conformal's marginal guarantee is retained. On ImageNet, PCC improves worst-class coverage on such classes by 0.058 [0.006, 0.110] at matched average set size, 42% of an oracle that sees the test labels. Of eight baselines on the same splits, six change the statistic by exactly zero and the best reaches 0.016 with an interval containing zero, so PCC is the only one distinguishable from no improvement; the gain persists with only 100 labelled classes out of 1000. A second finding concerns evaluation: worst-class coverage becomes unmeasurable before it becomes unachievable. Below roughly 35 test examples per class no improvement can be shown even for an oracle, so a null result there reflects the evaluation set, not the method. Restricting evaluation above this depth recovers a significant improvement on Pl@ntNet-300K, where the effect had appeared absent.

title: Local Evidence, Global Failure: Diagnosing Speech-Vision Temporal Composition in Audio-Visual Language Models
shortTitle: Local Evidence, Global Failure: Diagnosing Speech-Vision Temporal Composition in Audio-Visual Language Models
abstract: Audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) can fail at full-video speech-vision decisions even when useful visual evidence is locally recoverable. We introduce Temporal Evidence Decomposition (TED), a training-free diagnostic framework that separates local visual verification from speech-relative aggregation. Automatic speech recognition supplies a transcript and utterance interval. TED queries audio-free windows with the transcript for Temporal Alignment and Forecasting, or answer candidates for Cross-Modal Temporal Binding, then aggregates evidence relative to that interval. Across four frozen AV-LLMs on SVHalluc, Temporal Forecasting accuracy rises from 29.3-33.7% under full-video questioning to 79.3-82.2% with TED. Query replacement reduces recovery; the observed anchor remains beneficial when temporal-region availability is held fixed. Physical-isolation and timing-shortcut controls test alternative explanations. The findings distinguish locally recoverable evidence from successful full-video decisions, motivating explicit separation of narration content, utterance timing, and time-indexed visual evidence.

title: CHSM8: A Chess Transformer that Follows Natural-Language Style Prompts
shortTitle: CHSM8: A Chess Transformer that Follows Natural-Language Style Prompts
abstract: We present CHSM8, a 210M-parameter chess transformer that plays moves conditioned on a free-text description of a playing style, e.g. "go for the Sicilian Defense", "solid, safe, risk-free chess" or "You are Magnus Carlsen in his prime". The model is pretrained without search on 1.07B filtered Lichess games, using a factorized move representation and legal-move masking. It reaches 1837 Elo against a strength-limited Stockfish and, in 1,000-game matches, beat every other public model we tested that was likewise trained without preference tuning, rewards or search, including one with 13 times as many parameters. We then fine-tune it to follow text on a synthetic dataset: Gemma-4-31B describes the playing style of 3M game sides, a 1B Gemma-3 model distilled from the 2.4M of those descriptions that contradict nothing on the board labels the rest, and every one of 30M selected game sides gets five descriptions. Supervised fine-tuning attaches a frozen text encoder through gated cross-attention, and direct preference optimization (DPO) uses the same moves under a mismatched description as the rejected sample. After DPO, style adherence rises on every prompt we test (for example, queens traded early 53% -> 67%, pawn moves 29% -> 32% of all moves, queenside castling 97.3% -> 99.7%), and strength without a prompt stays within noise of SFT (1792 vs. 1797 Elo). Design choices at every stage were made by fixed-budget automated search loops on top of standard architectures and training recipes. We document the full pipeline and the decisions behind it, report the ablations that failed, and evaluate the models across many style prompts and kinds of games, with 1,000 games per setting. The work is fully open source and reproducible: weights, datasets with all training labels, prompts, configurations, inference code and playable demos are public and free to build on.

title: LateMatch: Breaking the Interaction Bottleneck via Cacheable Matching for Efficient Visual Localization
shortTitle: LateMatch: Breaking the Interaction Bottleneck via Cacheable Matching for Efficient Visual Localization
abstract: Visual localization is critical for embodied agents, but deploying state-of-the-art deep feature matchers on edge devices is fundamentally limited by their massive computational cost. Standard deep matchers tightly interleave intra-image context building and inter-image matching at every layer, creating a severe interaction bottleneck. Localizing a single query against K database images forces the system to execute the full network K independent times with no capacity for caching. To break this bottleneck, we advocate for a paradigm shift toward cacheable image matching. We realize this paradigm with LateMatch, a versatile approach that restructures existing matchers by deferring inter-image interaction to their final layers. By isolating intra-image processing into offline-cacheable Context Blocks, only a small set of Interaction Blocks must be executed online. To further optimize LateMatch, we introduce E-SToRE (Entropy-guided Spatial Token Reduction and Expansion). E-SToRE leverages the decreasing Shannon entropy of the late Interaction Blocks to dynamically reduce token counts just prior to cross-image interaction. Evaluated across HPatches, ScanNet, MegaDepth, ETH-3D, and Aachen, LateMatch reduces effective computational cost by over 2x compared to standard deep matchers, while E-SToRE yields an additional 10% to 14% savings with negligible degradation in accuracy.

title: CD-OPD: Contextual Digest for On-Policy Distillation
shortTitle: CD-OPD: Contextual Digest for On-Policy Distillation
abstract: Teacher takeover in on-policy distillation (OPD) can produce incorrect responses even when the student and teacher independently answer the same problem correctly, a failure we quantify using Collaboration Failure Rate (CFR). To address it, we propose Contextual Digest for On-Policy Distillation (CD-OPD). CD-OPD structures the earlier context of teacher guidance through a teacher-generated dependency graph, curating the required problem conditions and preceding reasoning as node summaries alongside the unchanged guidance in a Contextual Digest before student continuation. We further develop online meta-reweighting, which compares Digest segment gradients with a task gradient from independent student responses to improve student-only performance, favoring updates predicted to reduce task loss. Across eight benchmarks, CD-OPD improves average accuracy by 1.32--7.05 percentage points over representative existing OPD methods. It also reduces CFR by 27.4\%--56.4\% relative to existing takeover-based OPD methods.

title: Operator-Mismatch Contrastive Learning for World-Relative Trajectory Coherence
shortTitle: Operator-Mismatch Contrastive Learning for World-Relative Trajectory Coherence
abstract: World models are increasingly judged by how well they rank plausible futures, yet plausibility alone is the wrong target. The same scene can evolve under many latent rules, and a future that is smooth and physically valid under one rule can be incoherent under the rule actually in force. We formalize the resulting failure, operator-blindness, and show that it is systematically hidden by standard evaluation: a scorer can attain near-perfect generic ranking while separating current-world from other-world futures no better than chance. We introduce Operator-Mismatch Contrastive (OMC) learning, whose semantic hard negatives are valid-but-wrong-operator trajectories, and a matching protocol that measures world-relative coherence directly. On a controlled synthetic benchmark with in- and out-of-distribution operator parameters, across two trajectory-scoring backbones, and on feature-level external validation with CoPhy ballsCF, OMC raises operator-sensitive scoring far above a chance baseline that nonetheless achieves 0.99 generic top-1. We prove that the wrong-operator negative is necessary both for the protocol to detect the failure and for the objective to fix it, and position OMC as an auxiliary coherence signal (a trajectory-coherence scorer, not a generative model, planner, or control agent) that can be attached to existing world-model representations.

title: GreenNIDS: A Benchmark Workflow and Analysis Dataset for NetFlow Intrusion Detection Experiments
shortTitle: GreenNIDS: A Benchmark Workflow and Analysis Dataset for NetFlow Intrusion Detection Experiments
abstract: Comparing the predictive performance and computational cost of flow-based intrusion detection experiments requires both quantities to be available for each run. The run-level table combines predictive metrics with timing, throughput, memory use, and energy estimates based on thermal design power. A CPU-only demonstration comprises 216 runs across four dataset families, three versions, and binary and multiclass tasks. Ingestion produces a 216 x 96 analysis table with no duplicate run identifiers and complete Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) and F1 coverage. Multiclass ROC-AUC is missing for 36 PyTorch runs, making metric availability an explicit part of subsequent comparisons. The stored records support grouped performance and training-time plots, as well as resource screening after execution. Combining task-specific MCC thresholds with limits on training time, peak RAM, and estimated training energy retains 25.0% of the full run collection. These results establish compatibility within the evaluated collection and support comparisons after execution, subject to the recorded preprocessing, execution profile, and approximate energy accounting.

title: Painting Change Map as guidance for generating painting processes
shortTitle: Painting Change Map as guidance for generating painting processes
abstract: Digital art generation has undergone a massive paradigm shift, moving from static image synthesis to dynamic video generation that can mimic the human painting process. While existing models can synthesize visually stunning time-lapses of paintings being created or "unpainted," they largely treat the creative process as a black box. Current conditioning mechanisms are either too rigid, relying on static geometric cues like Canny edges or depth maps, or too holistic, utilizing simple scalar progress variables that offer no localized control. Consequently, users lack the agency to steer how a painting evolves over time. In this work, we argue that true control over the video generation of artwork requires a joint understanding of two fundamental dimensions: where an artist acts, and when those actions take place. To achieve this, we introduce the Painting Change Map, a novel spatio-temporal control mechanism that explicitly tracks normalized structural changes across a 1,000-timestep continuum, a resolution sufficient to capture fine-grained stroke-level changes while remaining computationally tractable. By mapping localized visual differences into an encoded RGB space, our representation enables fine-grained guidance for both the forward painting and reverse unpainting processes. Extensive benchmarking demonstrates the efficacy of our approach. We outperform existing control baselines and achieve competitive or superior results compared to state-of-the-art painting methods. Furthermore, under oracle conditions, our method surpasses all baselines by a significant margin. Code is available at https://github.com/Markus-Pobitzer/painting-change-map.

title: Multi-site Learning for Forecasting Day-Ahead Wind-Power Production for Onshore Wind Farms in Great Britain with Deep Neural Networks
shortTitle: Multi-site Learning for Forecasting Day-Ahead Wind-Power Production for Onshore Wind Farms in Great Britain with Deep Neural Networks
abstract: Accurate day-ahead wind-power production forecasting is increasingly important for energy system operations, market activity and balancing Great Britain's grid as wind generation grows. In this study, we train multi-site deep neural networks (DNNs) using pooled historical production and reanalysis weather data from 88 onshore wind Balancing Mechanism Units (BMUs). Forecasts are produced at 09:00 UK time for the following midnight-to-midnight delivery day, matching NESO's operational day-ahead forecasting schedule. We use reanalysis weather as future covariates during training and numerical weather prediction (NWP) forecasts during inference, extending training beyond the available historical NWP archive. Our multi-site recurrent neural network outperforms site-specific RNNs and a multi-site XGBoost model, while processing the full future-weather trajectory for the forecast horizon further improves accuracy relative to hour-aligned approaches. Our best model, an RNN with a bidirectional weather encoder (BiRNN) for NWP trajectory processing, reduces MW mean absolute error and root mean squared error relative to NESO by 17.94% and 12.51%, respectively, across 638,246 matched BMU-hour observations under conditions approximating unconstrained wind farm operations. In 40 leave-one-out trials, the BiRNN achieves lower MAE than NESO at 32 excluded sites, indicating transferable forecasting ability despite reduced accuracy when sites are omitted from training. title: Whistle and Wrong Lyrics: Synthetic Queries Are Not Enough for Real-World Query-by-Melody
shortTitle: Whistle and Wrong Lyrics: Synthetic Queries Are Not Enough for Real-World Query-by-Melody
abstract: People look up a song by humming it, but also by whistling it or singing it with the wrong words. Published query-by-humming systems and benchmarks focus on hums and sung queries, and no public dataset pairs whistles or wrong-lyrics singing with song recordings. We study both query types with a melody-only retrieval system: a key-normalized pitch track embedded by a 5.2M-parameter contour encoder, with a spectral-peak tracker for whistles. First, a physics-grounded generator renders synthetic whistles and nonsense-syllable singing from the vocal melodies of 11,083 songs. Training on them raises top-1 retrieval of held-out synthetic queries against an 11,050-song gallery from 0.180 to 0.251 for whistles and from 0.193 to 0.264 for wrong-lyrics singing, but the gain does not transfer: on the MLEnd test performers the best synthetic-only model gets 210 of 339 real whistles right at top-1, against 214 for the baseline. Second, a closed-set fine-tune on real MLEnd whistles with performer-disjoint splits raises whistle-to-hum top-1 from 0.631 (95% CI 0.581-0.681) to 0.673 (0.622-0.723), on known songs only. Third, two further generations of synthetic queries also fail to transfer: melody-conditioned whistles and la-la singing from a commercial neural music model leave real-whistle top-1 at 0.631, and an open-source pipeline (YingMusic-Singer-Plus singing with partly wrong, mumbled or nonsense lyrics, a DDSP whistle synthesizer, and a melody-error model fitted on real performers) gives at best 0.619 (paired difference -0.012, 95% CI -0.038 to +0.015). Across physics-based, commercial neural and open-source neural synthetic data, nothing transferred to real whistles, which points to collecting real queries as the missing step. title: MemDerive: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Agent Memory over Evolving Data
shortTitle: MemDerive: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Agent Memory over Evolving Data
abstract: Long-running agents rely on memory of their past interactions for task state, such as what has been completed and which conditions still hold. Such state is usually a derived state. No record states it, and it must be computed by rules from multiple records of an evolving history. Existing memory benchmarks score only the final answer, with no reference for the intermediate states behind it. A wrong answer therefore cannot be traced to the state that was missed, and a state that silently became outdated goes undetected. We present MemDerive, a diagnostic benchmark for agent memory over evolving data. It specifies each scenario symbolically, derives exact gold answers with Datalog, records the gold derivation DAG and the supporting events of every query, and renders the history in natural language with fictional entities and distractors. Its 10 scenarios contain 4,692 events and 1,503 queries whose difficulty varies along access, evolution, and composition. On this ground truth, MemDerive evaluates answer reliability, diagnoses failures by probing the nodes of the gold derivation DAG, and tracks whether answers stay correct as events arrive. Our evaluation of four memory systems reveals failures that final-answer benchmarks hide. On derived state, every memory system falls behind simple BM25 retrieval, although the same answer model reaches 96.01% when given the supporting events. Most failures are ungathered, as a system holds the missing intermediate state but does not retrieve it for the question that needs it. Memory systems also rarely propagate implicit changes, which no new record states. These results suggest three principles for memory design. Gather inputs along the derivation, store rules with their versions, and maintain derived states through recorded dependencies.

title: Mining the Self-Rewriting System: A Vision for Data Mining on AI-Native Infrastructure
shortTitle: Mining the Self-Rewriting System: A Vision for Data Mining on AI-Native Infrastructure
abstract: Classical data mining treats data as generated outside the learner. Emerging AI-native infrastructure invalidates this assumption: as agents observe system state, act, update retrieval stores and models, and promote new artifacts into the serving path, their own decisions reshape the future logs, traces, corpora, and evaluation records used for later training and release. We call this new research object a self-rewriting system and the resulting system-induced distribution shift endogenous drift. Our central, falsifiable claim is that cross-surface causes are not identifiable in general from marginal per-surface monitoring: different coupled failures can produce the same individual signals while differing in their joint behavior, requiring joint analysis for reliable attribution. This agenda comprises four foundational research problems: fusing heterogeneous drift signals into calibrated gating and attribution (C1); mining agent traces whose activity alphabet evolves (C2); maintaining knowledge fabrics through online reindexing, faithfulness, and compression decisions (C3); and safely promoting concurrent learning streams through one shared evaluation gate (C4). These remain fragmented across concept drift, performative prediction, process mining, streaming retrieval-augmented generation, and MLOps, without a unified data-mining agenda. We outline public benchmarks and evaluation criteria, using AI-native telecom only as a motivating exemplar with analogues in finance, software CI/CD, and clinical decision support.

title: TILDE: Teacher-in-the-Loop Distillation from Embodied Foundation Models
shortTitle: TILDE: Teacher-in-the-Loop Distillation from Embodied Foundation Models
abstract: Large-scale action pretraining equips Embodied Foundation Models (EFMs) with strong manipulation capabilities, with particular strengths in generalization and closed-loop robustness, but reproducing such pretraining requires substantial robot data and computation. To transfer these capabilities from pretrained EFMs to policies without action pretraining, we introduce TILDE (Teacher-In-the-Loop Distillation from EFMs), which synergizes on-policy distillation at student-induced states with learning from teacher-executed recovery trajectories. We further propose AutoDAgger, an autonomous data aggregation pipeline in which a robotic reward model is utilized to monitor task progress and trigger teacher intervention, thereby collecting recovery experience without human monitoring or manual control. AutoDAgger accelerates recovery-trajectory collection by more than $2\times$ compared with the human-in-the-loop method. By unifying learning from demonstrations, on-policy teacher supervision, and teacher's corrective behavior, TILDE improves task performance by up to $4.1\times$ over behavior cloning across three real-world tasks and supports effective cross-architecture distillation.

title: Simulating Infant Senses with Age-Tuned Networks
shortTitle: Simulating Infant Senses with Age-Tuned Networks
abstract: What a newborn sees, hears and feels, and how this changes month by month, has been measured sense by sense, with different methods and in different units. We bring these measurements together for the first two years of life and ask whether small neural networks tuned to a given age can turn them into a quick, inspectable simulation of sensory perception. Each sense's immaturity is written as a fixed, age-indexed filter on the input, and a small prediction network learns behind it over the first year. The filters alone reproduce the order in which the senses mature, by construction. The networks add what filters cannot: in vision they extract far less than their input allows at early stages (at the newborn stage a toy's position cannot be read out, $R^2 = 0.00$, against 0.57 for a network trained directly on the same input), and a critical period and perceptual narrowing emerge without being built in; in hearing they track what their input allows. The same filters drive the Baby Senses Lab, a free website that shows a user's own images and sounds as a baby of a chosen age might sense them. It is a research and teaching tool, not a diagnostic test.

title: Outcome-Anchored Credit Reallocation for Agentic Knowledge Graph Question Answering
shortTitle: Outcome-Anchored Credit Reallocation for Agentic Knowledge Graph Question Answering
abstract: Agentic knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) requires large language models (LLMs) to solve complex questions through multi-turn interactions with a knowledge graph (KG). Outcome-supervised reinforcement learning derives verifiable outcome rewards from final answers but uniformly assigns each rollout's outcome-level advantage to all policy-generated tokens, creating a trajectory-to-operation mismatch since KG operations within a rollout can have varying effects on the search process and final answer. To address this, we propose Outcome-Anchored Credit Reallocation (OACR), which employs a training-only KG-state outcome model to estimate outcome-reward changes between adjacent KG search states and converts them into operation credit, from which token-wise weights are derived. These multiplicative weights reallocate token-level update magnitudes while preserving the sign of the outcome-level advantage at every generated token. Across three benchmarks, OACR achieves stronger overall performance than existing KGQA methods while using fewer inference-time LLM calls and tokens.

title: Only Means Only: what a harmonization benchmark score averages over
shortTitle: Only Means Only: what a harmonization benchmark score averages over
abstract: Image harmonization methods adjust the colour and lighting of an object pasted into a photograph so that it looks native to its new scene, and they are ranked by average error on one benchmark whose test images are real photographs with one object recoloured. One photograph can yield several such test images, and the benchmark promises that no photograph appears in both the training and the test split. We find that 1,399 photographs do, and the composites built on them are a quarter of the test set. Duplicate checks over file names or bytes miss this, because every composite is a different file. On that quarter the three methods we score end to end read two to five times lower error than on the rest, but most of the gap is composition rather than the sharing: the shared composites come almost entirely from one of the benchmark's four source collections, and inside that collection the gap falls to about one and a half times. An official score is therefore an average over two populations, mixed in a proportion the benchmark does not report. We release a test list of 5,581 composites whose construction identities do not appear in training, with four confirmed near-duplicate pairs disclosed rather than removed, adoptable without retraining at the price of one rescore per checkpoint. We leave open whether the sharing itself changes what a model learns.

title: ATLAS: Attention-Guided Test-Time Latent Selection for Compositional Visual Autoregressive Generation
shortTitle: ATLAS: Attention-Guided Test-Time Latent Selection for Compositional Visual Autoregressive Generation
abstract: Visual autoregressive models produce convincing images but can misassign attributes and spatial relations. Searching multiple generation paths can improve composition, yet completing every candidate is costly. We introduce ATLAS, a training-free framework that uses the frozen generator's internal attention to guide search before final images are available. Within-prompt diagnostics identify attention-derived scores that predict final compositional preferences on Infinity, with category-dependent transfer to Switti. ATLAS uses these on-the-fly signals to progressively concentrate computation on promising trajectories. It maintains multiple coarse alternatives, prunes candidates without decoding at intermediate scales, and reserves image-space evaluation for a final choice among partial trajectories. ATLAS scales effectively on both backbones, achieving higher mean scores on the evaluated T2I-CompBench and GenEval categories as more computation is devoted to search. At the largest tested budget, the targeted T2I-CompBench mean improves by over 10% relative to each backbone. Separate profiles show over 50% less generation time than completing and evaluating all candidates at equal initial counts, alongside lower peak allocated GPU memory. Relative time savings are larger at the higher tested candidate count. Together, these results support scalable compositional search: additional sampling expands exploration, while attention-guided selection limits continuation cost without parameter updates or gradient-based optimization.

title: A 3D-Driven Framework for Moving-Camera Perspective-to-360° Video Generation
shortTitle: A 3D-Driven Framework for Moving-Camera Perspective-to-360° Video Generation
abstract: Turning a moving-camera perspective video into a 360° video requires more than just generating content outside the input frame: observations revealed over time must be preserved, unseen regions completed, and the resulting scene kept consistent as the camera viewpoint changes. Existing methods assign these different requirements to a single conditional video model, requiring them to be jointly learned from panoramic video data. We instead present a modular, 3D-driven framework that distributes these three responsibilities across specialized components, all connected through a shared scene representation. Input observations are reconstructed explicitly in 3D, while a pretrained panoramic image model completes unobserved content from a selected panoramic render. This generated content is lifted into the shared 3D scene, where it remains spatially anchored across camera viewpoints. Without requiring any additional panoramic-video training, our framework achieves state-of-the-art input-view fidelity, perceptual quality, and geometric consistency on a static-scene subset of the Argus evaluation set. These results support our decomposed, 3D-driven formulation as a promising alternative to direct video generation in this setting.

title: PolarVis: A Dataset and Diffusion Framework for RGB-to-Polarization Perception in Adverse Driving Scenes
shortTitle: PolarVis: A Dataset and Diffusion Framework for RGB-to-Polarization Perception in Adverse Driving Scenes
abstract: Reflections, glare, transparent structures, and material-dependent appearance variations can introduce ambiguity into RGB-based visual perception in vehicle-relevant environments. Polarization provides complementary reflection- and material-sensitive information, but its acquisition requires dedicated sensing hardware. This paper presents RGB-P Wild, a real-world dataset containing 10,000 paired RGB and four-angle linear-polarization image sets, together with PolarVis, a diffusion-based framework for recovering polarization representations from a single RGB image. PolarVis combines hierarchical RGB feature extraction, diffusion-based feature refinement, four angle-specific decoders, and multi-scale attention recalibration to reconstruct polarization intensity images at $0^\circ$, $45^\circ$, $90^\circ$, and $135^\circ$. On RGB-P Wild, PolarVis achieves a normalized-domain MSE of 0.0465, a PSNR of 27.83 dB, and an SSIM of 0.8597. Compared with the released PolarAnything model under the adopted evaluation protocol, PolarVis obtains an AoLP error of $25.66^\circ$ and a DoLP MAE of 0.0404, compared with $46.03^\circ$ and 0.1084, respectively. Cross-dataset evaluation on vehicle-mounted imagery further examines transfer beyond the training domain. In downstream evaluation, a frozen PCDNet achieves AP50/AP50:95 of 86.3%/59.1% on 990 RGBP-Car test images using PolarVis-generated polarization, compared with 87.0%/59.8% using measured polarization. These results indicate that RGB-derived polarization retains useful polarimetric information for the evaluated perception tasks, while remaining distinct from calibrated physical polarization measurements.

title: Visual-Inertial Odometry for Ground Robots with Dynamic Camera-IMU Extrinsic Calibration
shortTitle: Visual-Inertial Odometry for Ground Robots with Dynamic Camera-IMU Extrinsic Calibration

title: From Unverifiable Domain Text to Cross-Lingual RLVR via Code-Switched Task Synthesis
shortTitle: From Unverifiable Domain Text to Cross-Lingual RLVR via Code-Switched Task Synthesis

title: RAHF-Net: Range-Aware Heterogeneous Fusion for LiDAR-Assisted RGB Semantic Segmentation
shortTitle: RAHF-Net: Range-Aware Heterogeneous Fusion for LiDAR-Assisted RGB Semantic Segmentation
abstract: This paper studies LiDAR-assisted RGB semantic segmentation, where LiDAR point-cloud features improve dense pixel-wise predictions in the RGB image plane rather than 3D point labels or detections. A Range-Aware Heterogeneous Fusion (RAHF) module then uses a soft depth-derived range mask to perform LiDAR-guided geometric enhancement in reliable near-field regions and visual-context enhancement in sparse far-field regions. On KITTI-360, RAHF-Net achieves 65.76 mIoU, outperforming representative RGB-only and RGB-LiDAR baselines, including CMX by 1.45 points. title: Energy-Score Stabilized Attentive Mixture-Density Policy: A Lightweight Approach to Multimodal Robot Motion
shortTitle: Energy-Score Stabilized Attentive Mixture-Density Policy: A Lightweight Approach to Multimodal Robot Motion
abstract: For practical motion generation, it is essential to handle multimodality (multiple actions can be correct for the same observation) while maintaining low inference cost and strong generalization from limited demonstrations. Concretely, we output Gaussian mixture parameters for joint commands (and optionally attention points) and optimize them with the Energy Score (computed as a sum of 1D CRPS under a diagonal covariance assumption) instead of the negative log-likelihood (NLL) to avoid MDN singularities and gradient-scale instabilities. Our architecture couples explicit spatial attention with mixture-density outputs, enabling robust multimodal behavior selection under visual noise and small-data regimes. On an 8-DOF manipulator, the method generates distinct avoidance trajectories and stabilizes learning in obstacle avoidance. Moreover, in a randomized moving-object grasping task, where spatiotemporal multimodality and fast timing decisions are required, the proposed model outperforms Diffusion Policy by 15-25% under several unseen conditions, demonstrating superior generalization and real-time feasibility.

title: When Form Changes but Logic Doesn't: Building Logic-invariant LLMs through Logical Structure
shortTitle: When Form Changes but Logic Doesn't: Building Logic-invariant LLMs through Logical Structure
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance across diverse reasoning tasks, yet it remains unclear whether this performance reflects an understanding of underlying logical structure or a reliance on shallow semantic cues. A key indicator of such understanding is whether models treat logically equivalent inputs consistently, producing the same predictions despite differences in expression. Through systematic evaluation on curated data, we show that even strong LLMs often fail this test: they do not consistently preserve predictions across logically equivalent inputs and generalize poorly to unseen logical forms. To address this limitation, we propose LoGIcal STructure-guided reasoning (LoGIST), a framework that guides LLM reasoning with explicit logical structure. LoGIST maps each input instance to a decision diagram, a directed acyclic graph that captures the underlying logical structure, and encodes this graph into a logical embedding that conditions the LLM's reasoning process. Across multiple training settings, LoGIST reduces inconsistency under logical equivalence and improves generalization to unseen logical forms, suggesting that logical invariance is a useful target for building more robust and generalizable logical reasoning in LLMs.

title: MT Forcing: Towards Stable and Consistent Multi-Turn Image Editing with Autoregressive Diffusion
shortTitle: MT Forcing: Towards Stable and Consistent Multi-Turn Image Editing with Autoregressive Diffusion
abstract: Multi-turn image editing aims to modify an image according to a sequence of instructions, enabling more effective interactive visual content creation for users. However, existing methods often exhibit noticeable drift after only a few editing turns, manifesting in two aspects: 1) unstable visual quality, with accumulating artifacts and degraded details; and 2) inconsistent image content, with unintended changes to preserved regions and prior edits. To address these challenges, we propose MT Forcing, a novel training paradigm for multi-turn image editing with unified multimodal models (UMMs) based on autoregressive diffusion. Specifically, we propose Single-Turn Distribution Matching Distillation (Single-Turn DMD), which supervises student self-rollouts with a teacher that applies cumulative edits to the source image in a single turn, providing visual-quality guidance without recursive error accumulation. Additionally, we introduce Teacher-Forcing Guidance, which supervises history-dependent transitions on reference trajectories during warmup and as a regularizer during distillation, encouraging cross-turn content consistency beyond what per-turn distribution matching alone can ensure. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the multi-turn image editing capabilities of UMMs, yielding more stable visual quality and stronger cross-turn consistency.

title: Towards Figurative Language Understanding in Moroccan Darija: An Evaluation of Large Language Models
shortTitle: Towards Figurative Language Understanding in Moroccan Darija: An Evaluation of Large Language Models

Our findings reveal that closed-weight models achieve the strongest translation performance, while the benefits of contextual information vary across models and tasks. title: AeroDASH: Asynchronous Vision-Language-Action Control for Continuous UAV Flight
shortTitle: AeroDASH: Asynchronous Vision-Language-Action Control for Continuous UAV Flight

title: UniState: Unifying Memory and Intervention for Controllable World Simulation
shortTitle: UniState: Unifying Memory and Intervention for Controllable World Simulation
abstract: World models offer increasingly rich environments for exploration, yet intervening in a world while observing the consequences from freely chosen viewpoints remains challenging. We develop training and sampling strategies that help generated videos follow the specified object motion and camera trajectory while preserving this capacity to generate responses beyond the prescribed transformations. title: From Label Priors to Task Evidence: Efficient Long-Video Frame Selection via Bayesian GRPO
shortTitle: From Label Priors to Task Evidence: Efficient Long-Video Frame Selection via Bayesian GRPO
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) face significant scalability challenges in long-video understanding due to quadratic attention complexity and context window constraints. Existing retrieval-based approaches typically rely on supervised learning from static keyframe annotations. However, these label priors often fail to align with the actual information required by downstream MLLMs for complex reasoning, creating a misalignment between the training target and inference needs. To bridge this gap, we propose a probabilistic framework that reformulates frame selection as latent-variable inference. We first initialize a lightweight policy using supervised learning to capture general visual saliency. Then, we treat a frozen MLLM as a task environment and use its answer likelihood as dense task evidence to refine the policy via Bayesian Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Within this formulation, the negative log-likelihood (NLL) over ground-truth answer tokens provides a principled dense reward, while a prior-matching KL term preserves semantic consistency with the elicited label prior. This process transitions the selection principle from static label priors to task evidence. Extensive experiments on Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench demonstrate that our selector achieves competitive accuracy with MLLM-based scorers while retaining the inference efficiency of lightweight methods. The selector is trained once with a frozen MLLM environment and transfers directly to multiple downstream MLLMs without retraining. title: Mixture-of-Memories: Low-Overhead Language Modeling with Modular Knowledge Injection
shortTitle: Mixture-of-Memories: Low-Overhead Language Modeling with Modular Knowledge Injection
abstract: Large language models store substantial factual knowledge in their parameters, yet this knowledge is difficult to control, update, and reliably elicit at inference time. Existing memory-augmented approaches typically rely on a single auxiliary mechanism, such as retrieval, parameter updates, or neural memory, and therefore apply the same form of correction to tokens with very different knowledge demands. We propose Mixture-of-Memories (MoM), a memory-augmented language modeling framework that separates routed neural memory from writable factual memory. MoM combines a frozen base LM with two neural memory experts: a latent memory that provides low-latency hidden-state corrections and a lexical memory that provides a token-space knowledge pathway. A lightweight Budget Router sets per-token mixture weights from uncertainty and disagreement features, replacing the fixed interpolation of prior memory modules. For post-hoc updates, an external explicit memory stays outside the router, because a router trained before facts are written learns to down-weight it; new facts are appended without retraining any component and used only when an answer-level gate accepts the retrieved fact. Experiments across language modeling, factual QA, update analysis, and efficiency show that MoM improves both predictive accuracy and updateability while retaining low inference overhead.

title: SurGPT: A Multi-Task Foundation Model for Robotic Surgical Skills Assessment and Gesture Recognition
shortTitle: SurGPT: A Multi-Task Foundation Model for Robotic Surgical Skills Assessment and Gesture Recognition
abstract: The assessment of surgical skills in robotic surgery training has traditionally relied on subjective evaluations by human experts, creating bottlenecks in surgical education and limiting scalability. We present a novel foundation model that automatically analyzes robotic surgical videos to provide comprehensive skill assessment and gesture understanding. Combining a visual encoder with a transformer architecture, the model performs three key tasks simultaneously: 1) surgical task classification (knot tying, needle passing, suturing), 2) skill level assessment on a standardized scale, and 3) natural language generation of surgical gesture descriptions. The model processes video sequences from the da Vinci surgical robot and generates human-readable text descriptions of surgical actions, similar to how language models generate text from prompts, using a multi-task learning framework with adaptive uncertainty weighting to optimize performance across all objectives. Our transformer-based architecture incorporates positional encoding for temporal understanding and attention mechanisms for spatiotemporal feature integration. Evaluated on the da Vinci Skills Simulator dataset, the proposed framework demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in surgical task recognition and provides interpretable skill assessments that correlate with expert evaluations, with the model's ability to generate natural language descriptions of surgical gestures opening new possibilities for automated surgical education, real-time feedback systems, and objective skill assessment in surgical training and certification programs.

title: Preserving the Manifold: Frozen Expert Alignment for Label-Efficient SAR Scene Understanding
shortTitle: Preserving the Manifold: Frozen Expert Alignment for Label-Efficient SAR Scene Understanding
abstract: Cross-modal alignment of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery to natural language is constrained by two distinct failures. The first is modality mismatch: text encoders pre-trained on optical imagery, such as CLIP, cannot be efficiently fine-tuned on SAR, because active microwave backscatter is physically incompatible with passive optical reflectance and the available SAR caption datasets are orders of magnitude too small to bridge this gap without substantially degrading the learned semantic manifold. The second is physical forgetting: SAR encoders pre-trained on large-scale self-supervised objectives encode radar physics that are progressively erased when the encoder is fine-tuned for text alignment on limited caption data. A single design principle addresses both failures: keep both encoders frozen and learn only a constrained, structure-preserving bridge. Our Frozen Expert framework aligns a frozen CROMA SAR encoder with a frozen CLIP text encoder via a lightweight constrained residual bridge. We formally define physical forgetting via Procrustes disparity and show our bridge preserves SAR geometry significantly better than fine-tuning (disparity: 0.210 vs. 0.351). We validate generality across multiple SAR backbones and text encoders. On zero-shot SAR scene classification, our approach outperforms fine-tuned baselines using up to 8x less training data: DFC2020 (+10.3% R@1, +15.5% mAP), EuroSAT-SAR (+15.7% R@1, +12.2% mAP), BigEarthNet-MM (+14.7% R@1). These results establish frozen manifold alignment as a principled, data-efficient alternative to fine-tuning in high-disparity cross-modal settings.

title: MOSAIC: Multi-Objective Search for Allocating Inference Cache Across LLM Decoder Layers
shortTitle: MOSAIC: Multi-Objective Search for Allocating Inference Cache Across LLM Decoder Layers
abstract: The Key-Value (KV) cache is the main memory bottleneck of long-context LLM inference. Token eviction methods such as SnapKV, H2O, AdaKV and L2Norm shrink it, but they give every transformer layer the same budget, although layers differ in which tokens they need. We present MOSAIC, a multi-objective neural architecture search that learns per-layer KV-cache budgets for any eviction method. One search maps the trade-off between average budget and task score; its best allocation transfers to every target budget without further search, and an optional budget-constrained search refines it. Across four eviction methods on Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2, MOSAIC beats uniform allocation in 146 of 154 (task, method, budget) settings, by up to +48 points on RULER and +11.9 on LongBench (LCC). On both models, it reaches the score of uniform allocation with up to 4x less KV cache (75% smaller). Against EvolKV, MOSAIC explores a ~10^40 x larger search space with 4x fewer evaluations and 18% fewer GPU-hours per budget, and scores higher in 5 of 6 settings. The learned allocations consistently favour a small set of middle layers.

title: RARE: Reinforcement Learning with Adaptive Rubric Evolution for Open-Ended Generation
shortTitle: RARE: Reinforcement Learning with Adaptive Rubric Evolution for Open-Ended Generation
abstract: Verifiable rewards have advanced reinforcement learning in mathematics and code. However, many valuable open-ended tasks share three properties: no automatic verifier of overall quality, multiple requirements to satisfy jointly, and multiple valid responses to each query. Training therefore needs feedback on requirement satisfaction across different valid responses. Rubric-based reinforcement learning provides this feedback by aggregating scores from explicit criteria. As learning progresses unevenly, some criteria become fully satisfied and lose discrimination while others remain informative. Dynamic methods revise shared rubrics or select evolving criteria to restore discrimination, but may also change useful criteria. To address this, we propose Reinforcement Learning with Adaptive Rubric Evolution (RARE). The core idea is to use current policy feedback to guide both which criteria change and what their replacements assess. Sample-level updates replace criteria fully satisfied across current outputs with checks of remaining quality differences, retaining all other criteria and scores. Within this rule, we compare rewarding desirable qualities with penalizing observed flaws. Video script generation exemplifies these properties and supports content production. Its demands for coherent, executable narratives under constraints make it a challenging testbed. Targeting flaws performs best across three video types with a mean gain of 3.82 points over matched static rubrics. Model and human preferences support these gains. Improvements also extend to writing and general generation benchmarks.

title: Intent-Informed Model Predictive Control for Shared Autonomy in Remote Manipulation Tasks
shortTitle: Intent-Informed Model Predictive Control for Shared Autonomy in Remote Manipulation Tasks
abstract: Shared autonomy is a control paradigm that combines human cognitive abilities with robot precision to enable effective remote manipulation in complex environments. A key challenge is how to adapt the level of autonomy using information extracted from the human, task, and/or environment. In this paper, we propose a novel arbitration strategy that dynamically adjusts the level of autonomy in the system using the entropy of a belief distribution derived from a multimodal intent inference. Human intent is modeled with a Dynamic Bayesian Network (DBN), which updates beliefs over goals given real-time operator gaze data and robot arm motion during teleoperation. We then formulate the blending of human input and autonomous control as a Model Predictive Control (MPC) problem, where the system's autonomous behavior is guided by the belief distribution. This approach enables continuous, gradual transitions across the full spectrum of autonomy levels, from direct teleoperation to full autonomy. To validate our approach, we conducted experiments to compare the performance of our proposed algorithm against two MPC-based shared autonomy methods. Compared to the baselines, our approach achieved reductions of at least 61% in object retrieval time, 44% in trajectory length, and 60% in human control input. Participants reported high perceived control, predictability, intent recognition, and responsiveness, along with low workload.

title: DragonMoCap: Monocular Video-based Motion Capture for Diverse Dragon Topologies
shortTitle: DragonMoCap: Monocular Video-based Motion Capture for Diverse Dragon Topologies
abstract: This work explores monocular motion capture for dragon-type characters, which currently relies on manual keyframing due to the lack of high-quality datasets and parametric models. The primary obstacle lies in the extreme topological diversity across dragon rigs, where varying joint counts and naming conventions render traditional fixed-template regressors inapplicable. To address this, we introduce DragonMoCap, a novel framework that treats the target rig as a dynamic input rather than a fixed prior. By deliberately scoping the framework to the most prevalent production topologies, we ensure high-fidelity results across diverse morphologies. The core of our approach is the design of language-grounded joint query tokens, which establish a dual-property representation: ensuring intra-rig discriminability while maintaining cross-rig similarity. We further propose a non-parametric query-token retrieval mechanism to enable zero-shot adaptation to unseen rigs without retraining. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that DragonMoCap consistently outperforms HMR-style baselines across diverse dragon topologies. The practical utility of our framework is further evidenced by its integration into professional animation workflows, highlighting its potential for real-time industrial applications.
